lines: Cold air, a scary moment, or a great song can all give you goosebumps.
Under your skin, each hair grows from a follicle.
Attached to the side of each follicle is a tiny muscle, the {arrector|AH0 R EH1 K T ER0} {pili|P AY1 L AY0}.
Your sympathetic nerves, part of *fight or flight*, send it a signal.
The muscle contracts. It pulls the hair upright and tugs the skin into a little bump.
The name comes from the skin of a plucked goose.
In furry animals, raised fur traps a layer of warm air against the skin.
It also makes a scared animal look *bigger*.
Humans have too little body hair for this to warm us. [pause 100] The reflex is mostly a leftover.
But in mice, the same nerve and muscle help wake hair stem cells during long cold spells.
And the song? [pause 150] Strong emotions can fire the same signal, so you get *chills*.
